newsitem.title: GEORGIA: SOCCER-GASCOIGNE SURVIVES FIERCE TEST OF CHARACTER.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-GASCOIGNE SURVIVES FIERCE TEST OF CHARACTER.

text.p: Paul Gascoigne might well be a self-confessed wife-beater, but he showed on Saturday that despite his well-documented human failings he is still an outstanding footballer.

Born-again Christian Glenn Hoddle, the England coach who ignored demands by women's groups to drop Gascoigne, picking him instead to play in Saturday's 2-0 World Cup qualifying win over Georgia, praised him for his midfield performance which anchored England's win.

Hoddle has never condoned Gascoigne's attack on his wife Sheryl, but he has encouraged the volatile 29-year-old to be counselled in an attempt to curb some of the wilder excesses of his personality which years ago prompted former England coach Bobby Robson to describe him as being "daft as a brush."

But on Saturday, in the hostile atmosphere of the Boris Paichadze Stadium, Gascoigne gave a mature, disciplined performance that was a huge improvement on the way he played against Poland in England's last qualifier.
Hoddle was full of praise for him afterwards.
"He has coped extremely well," said the England coach. "And to be fair the other players have been fantastic around him.
"I have seen improvement in him already. I'm not saying he is the finished article, but he's shown people he is trying to change. But he is doing it without it affecting him as a footballer.

"I had to put my football head on and I've been proved correct. He was under a lot of pressure but has come through it. I think it did take him 10 minutes to settle into his game, but he came through.
"I have seen signs of maturity in him. I'm paid to pick the team and, though you are not always going to be right, it's good to be this time.
"He played with his head not his heart."
While it was not a vintage, virtuoso performance, Gascoigne showed the class that has always singled him out as a special player.

There was no clowning around and not too many signs of the old, impish "Gazza". Instead there was the odd flick here, the little trick there, but Gascoigne curbed the excesses and instead played some thoughtful, useful football which benefited not only himself but his team.
"Further down the line, what we want to see is him playing more and more like that," said Hoddle, adding, "At the end, we have all got our rewards."
Hoddle was also delighted that England, without skipper Alan Shearer, recovering from a groin injury, won with first-half goals from Teddy Sheringham and Les Ferdinand.
Those goals made it three wins out of three since Hoddle took control of the team after Euro 96 and means they top their qualifying group by three points over Italy, who have played a match less.

"We've now got a psychological advantage when we play Italy in February -- I can have a good Christmas now," said Hoddle, part of the England team that won 1-0 on the same ground against the old Soviet Union 10 years ago.
A victory for England, and a personal success for Gascoigne who now just has to bring some order and maturity to his life off the field to match the apparent improvement he has started to make on it.
